prize_parts.citation: for the prediction of flat moire bands in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states at the magic angle

statement.case_for: The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model gives a simple, general mechanism: interference between two slightly rotated lattices flattens the bands at a magic angle, and strong correlations follow. The 2018 experiments by the Jarillo-Herrero group then found correlated insulators and superconductivity exactly where the theory said to look. Many independent groups and platforms (twisted multilayers, transition-metal dichalcogenide moire systems, fractional Chern insulators) have reproduced and extended this. It is a clean case of theory preceding experiment and opening a new field of tunable correlated matter, with a minimal model that can be analysed and tested, which is the kind of discovery I most value. The 2010 graphene prize concerned a different phenomenon, so there is no overlap.
statement.case_against: The honest reservation is maturity and attribution. The origin of the superconducting pairing and of the correlated phases is still debated, so a citation must rest on the flat bands and the correlated states, not on a mechanism. Yuan Cao, first author of the 2018 papers, and the groups that confirmed the effect early (Dean, Yacoby, Young, and others) are outside a three-person limit, which is a real fairness problem. A committee that prefers longer verification could reasonably say this is about five to ten years early.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp Z2 topological insulator first, as a mature, quantitatively verified concept with nearly two decades of confirmation, and ranks magic-angle graphene second while noting the pairing mechanism is unsettled.
responses.response: I agree with the maturity point and share the ranking of B018 and B022 at the top, so we differ mostly on timing, not on quality. Where I disagree is on the weight of the unsettled superconductivity. The flat-band prediction and the observation of correlated insulators do not depend on the pairing mechanism, and the effect has been reproduced across many platforms in a few years. B018 is the safer choice on maturity, but the 2016 prize on topological phases partly covers its conceptual ground, and its attribution problem (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and the Fu-Kane three-dimensional extension) is no easier than the Cao problem for B022. I keep B018 as my first alternative and do not regard it as clearly ahead.

responses.point: Kroll puts the optical lattice clock first: a hundredfold improvement over the caesium standard, a concrete measurement idea (magic wavelength), many independent reproductions, and a redefinition of the second under way.
responses.response: Kroll's case is strong and B012 is the most broadly supported candidate in the whole committee, so I take it seriously. Its attribution is also cleaner than for any condensed-matter candidate, with two names and a clear split between concept and demonstration. My reservation is not about quality but about the kind of advance. It is a decisive improvement in an established measurement, building on the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes, while twisted graphene opens a new class of phenomena. I would not argue strongly against B012 and I rank it as my second alternative. If our discussion shows that the committee puts accuracy of attribution and maturity first, it is the consensus choice and I could accept it.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first and also supports Z2 topological insulators, and calls the magic-angle prize 'a bit early' because the interpretation of superconductivity and correlated phases is still debated.
responses.response: I take the 'a bit early' remark seriously, and it is the best argument against my own first choice. My reply is that the existence of the flat bands, of the correlated insulators and of superconductivity is well established. What is debated is the pairing mechanism, and prizes have often been given while mechanism questions were open. I am less convinced that circuit QED (B064) outranks the condensed-matter candidates for me: it is clearly foundational for superconducting processors, but its support in the committee is thin (a single first-place vote), and the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits already recognises that area. I would like to hear whether the 2025 prize reduces the room for B064.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron optics first as a verified instrument invention, and ranks magic-angle graphene second while pointing out that Yuan Cao is not among the credited names.
responses.response: I agree with the Cao point and treat it as the main fairness issue for B022. I do not think it blocks the prize: the three-person limit forces such omissions in nearly every case, and the theory-plus-experiment pairing of Bistritzer-MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero is the natural configuration. On B032, the instrument case is real but I am concerned that only one member ranks it, and I cannot judge from my own field whether the Rose-Haider-Krivanek split is fully fair. I would ask Olsson to say what the decisive contribution of each of the three was and whether Knoll and others should weigh into the credit before the committee considers it further.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the unsettled pairing mechanism in magic-angle graphene to make the prize premature.
How to handle the omission of Yuan Cao and early confirming groups under a three-person limit.
Whether B012 is simply the stronger consensus case, given its support from all eight opening ballots, if we weigh maturity and clean attribution above novelty of the physics.
Whether the 2016 topological phases prize leaves enough room for B018.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile: I have no listed collaboration, institutional tie or supervision relation with any of the credited names on the shortlist. My expertise is in statistical physics of complex systems, so I am not an expert on the experimental detail of the atomic, particle and astroparticle candidates and defer to colleagues there.
